content: Iron oxide refers to a group of chemical compounds composed of iron and oxygen. There are sixteen known types of iron oxides and oxyhydroxides, each with distinct chemical and physical properties. Oxides: 1. Iron(II) oxide (FeO), also known as wüstite in its mineral form, is a black oxide. When in powdered form, it is highly reactive and can ignite easily, posing a risk of explosion. 2. Iron(II,III) oxide (Fe3O4), commonly referred to as magnetite or lodestone in its mineral form, is a mixed-valence compound. It is a significant iron ore and forms readily when iron oxidizes in underwater environments, such as inside tanks or below the waterline of ships. 3. Iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3) exists in two forms: hematite (α-Fe2O3) and maghemite (γ-Fe2O3). Hematite is a major component of rust, while maghemite is a less common mineral form. Industrially, purified iron(III) oxide is known as rouge and is used as a coating in magnetic audio and computer media. In dry or alkaline conditions, it can cause passivation, which inhibits further rusting. Hydroxides: 1. Iron(II) hydroxide (Fe(OH)2) is a compound formed by the reaction of iron(II) ions with hydroxide ions. 2. Iron(III) hydroxide (Fe(OH)3), also known as bernalite, is a hydrated form of iron(III) oxide. Oxide-Hydroxides: 1. Goethite (α-FeOOH) is a naturally occurring iron oxyhydroxide mineral. 2. Akaganéite (β-FeOOH) is another polymorph of iron oxyhydroxide, often found in chloride-rich environments. 3. Lepidocrocite (γ-FeOOH) is a polymorph of goethite and akaganéite, commonly associated with rust. 4. 5. Ferrihydrite (Fe5HO8·4H2O) is an amorphous iron oxyhydroxide with a variable composition. 6. 7. Schwertmannite is a poorly crystalline iron oxyhydroxide that forms in acidic, sulfate-rich environments. 8. Green rusts are layered double hydroxides containing iron in both the +2 and +3 oxidation states. Uses: Iron oxides have a wide range of applications, particularly in ceramics and pigments. In ceramic glazes, iron oxides contribute to the coloration after firing at high temperatures. Natural iron oxide pigments, known as ochers, have been used in art since prehistoric times, including in the famous cave paintings at Lascaux. Common pigments derived from iron oxides include raw and burnt siennas and umbers. These pigments are primarily composed of iron(III) oxide, which is red or rust-colored, while iron(II) oxide pigments are typically black. In the cosmetic industry, iron oxide pigments are widely used due to their non-toxic, moisture-resistant, and non-bleeding properties. Magnetite, marketed as Black Oxide, is used to coat steel tools, providing corrosion resistance and an aesthetically pleasing finish. Properties: 1. Iron(II) oxide (FeO) is a black powder that is highly reactive and can ignite spontaneously, making it a potential safety hazard. 2. Iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3), in its alpha form (hematite), is a major component of rust. In its gamma form (maghemite), it is less common. Purified iron(III) oxide, known as rouge, is used in magnetic coatings for audio and computer media. It can inhibit rust formation in dry or alkaline environments. 3. Iron(II,III) oxide (Fe3O4), or magnetite, is a naturally magnetic mineral and a significant source of iron ore. It forms readily in underwater environments and is commonly found in ship hulls or tanks. Compared to other abundant elements like aluminum and titanium, iron is relatively easy to extract from its ores.
